claim: Appendicular motoneurons project into the hindlimb buds as soon as the latter begin to emerge at stage 48.
source: Appendicular MNs already project into the hindlimb buds as soon as the latter begin to emerge at stage 48 (van Mier et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Mier et al., 1985

claim: At stage 50, the nascent limb consists of a tissue protrusion that is visible on the ventral side of the rostral tail myotomes, next to the larva's abdomen.
source: At stage 50, the nascent limb consists of a tissue protrusion that is visible on the ventral side of the rostral tail myotomes, next to the larva's abdomen (Nieuwkoop and Faber, 1956).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nieuwkoop and Faber, 1956

claim: During the pre-metamorphic period, the animal triples in size.
source: The limb bud then continues to grow and differentiate throughout the pre-metamorphic period, during which time the animal triples in size (Figure 1A1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A1 showing size differences

claim: At stage 56/57, the adult-like hindlimb is formed with differentiated thigh and leg segments along with the appearance of five webbed toes.
source: At stage 56/57, the adult-like hindlimb is formed with differentiated thigh and leg segments along with the appearance of five webbed toes (Figure 1A2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A2 showing morphological changes

claim: The limb extensor and flexor muscle groups are differentiated at stage 56/57.
source: The limb extensor and flexor muscle groups are also differentiated at this time.
evidence: Stated as observation at stage 56/57

claim: The axial motor column is distributed ventro-medially along the entire length of the spinal cord.
source: Specifically, the axial motor column is distributed ventro-medially along the entire length of the spinal cord, whereas the hindlimb motor column is located more medio-laterally and restricted to spinal segments 7 to 9, identified by counting caudally the number of ventral roots from the obex (Figure 1B–D), as reported previously (Hulshof et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1B-D and citation to Hulshof et al., 1987

claim: The hindlimb motor column is located more medio-laterally and restricted to spinal segments 7 to 9.
source: Specifically, the axial motor column is distributed ventro-medially along the entire length of the spinal cord, whereas the hindlimb motor column is located more medio-laterally and restricted to spinal segments 7 to 9, identified by counting caudally the number of ventral roots from the obex (Figure 1B–D), as reported previously (Hulshof et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1B-D and citation to Hulshof et al., 1987

claim: In early stages 50-52, appendicular motoneurons have relatively small cell bodies (<10 µm) and a reduced dendritic arbor.
source: In early stages 50–52 (Figure 1B1, B2), retrograde labeling from the limb bud revealed a high density of MNs with relatively small cell bodies (<10 µm) and a reduced dendritic arbor, located more dorso-laterally than the axial MNs.
evidence: Supported by retrograde labeling data shown in Figure 1B1, B2

claim: From stage 55 onward, appendicular motoneuron somata become bigger (20-50 µm) and acquire a characteristic elongated cell body shape and extended dendritic arbor.
source: From stage 55 onward (Figure 1C) the appendicular motor column is positioned more laterally due to the enlargement of these spinal segments with a lower neuronal density. The appendicular MN somata then become bigger (20–50 µm) and acquire a characteristic elongated cell body shape and extended dendritic arbor, extending from a ventro-medial to dorso-lateral region of the hemicord (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C

claim: At stage 53, appendicular motoneurons were not labeled with ChAT and VAChT antibodies.
source: At stage 53 (Figure 2A), appendicular MNs were not labeled at all with the ChAT and VAChT antibodies, whereas in the same spinal slices, axial MNs were strongly positive for the two proteins.
evidence: Supported by immunochemistry data shown in Figure 2A

claim: At stage 53, axial motoneurons were strongly positive for ChAT and VAChT.
source: At stage 53 (Figure 2A), appendicular MNs were not labeled at all with the ChAT and VAChT antibodies, whereas in the same spinal slices, axial MNs were strongly positive for the two proteins.
evidence: Supported by immunochemistry data shown in Figure 2A

claim: At stage 57, both ChAT and VAChT were clearly expressed in appendicular motoneurons.
source: In contrast, at later stages (e.g., stage 57 in Figure 2B) both ChAT and VAChT were clearly expressed in appendicular MNs (see lower left insets) as well as in axial MNs.
evidence: Supported by immunochemistry data shown in Figure 2B

claim: ChAT and VAChT were not immuno-detected in appendicular motoneurons until stage 55.
source: Overall, ChAT and VAChT were not immuno-detected in appendicular MNs until stage 55, in contrast to axial MNs which were immunoreactive throughout the early pre-metamorphic stages.
evidence: Supported by immunochemistry data across developmental stages

claim: Axial motoneurons were immunoreactive for ChAT and VAChT throughout the early pre-metamorphic stages.
source: Overall, ChAT and VAChT were not immuno-detected in appendicular MNs until stage 55, in contrast to axial MNs which were immunoreactive throughout the early pre-metamorphic stages.
evidence: Supported by immunochemistry data across developmental stages

claim: The immuno-signal for ChAT and VAChT detected in the appendicular motor column at stages 49-54 was not significantly higher than the background signal level.
source: The fluorescence variation (∆F/F) measured at stages 49–54 showed that the immuno-signal detected in the appendicular motor column was not significantly higher than the background signal level (ChAT: 13.5 ± 5.5 at stage 49–51; 1.2 ± 1.0 at stage 52–54; VAChT: 1.3 ± 0.8 at stage 49–51; 5.2 ± 2.0 at stage 52–54; Figure 2C, right).
evidence: Supported by quantitative fluorescence analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: At stage 55-57, the appendicular/axial fluorescence variation for ChAT and VAChT increased to approximately 20%.
source: Immuno-labeling in the LMC became more robust with further larval development, with the appendicular/axial fluorescence variation increasing to ~20% (at stage 55–57; ChAT: 120.4 ± 31.8; VAChT: 72.4 ± 3.9; Figure 2C, right), which was consistent with the clear detection of both ChAT and VAChT in appendicular MNs at the later pre-metamorphic stages.
evidence: Supported by quantitative fluorescence analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: No ChAT mRNA signal was detected in the appendicular motor column area in stages 49-52.
source: No signal was detected in the appendicular motor column area in stages 49–52 (Figure 2D left; n = 7).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D

claim: A ChAT ISH signal was weakly detectable from stage 53-54.
source: A ChAT ISH signal was then weakly detectable from stage 53–54 (n = 2), to become strongly evident from stage 55 onwards (Figure 2D right; n = 7).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D

claim: A strong ChAT ISH signal was observed in axial motoneurons throughout the entire developmental period examined.
source: In contrast, a strong ChAT ISH signal was observed in axial MNs throughout the entire developmental period examined.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data

claim: Some ChAT-positive motoneurons at stage 62 were co-labeled with retrograde fluorescent dye previously applied at stage 51/52.
source: Significantly, some of these ChAT-positive MNs were also co-labeled with the retrograde fluorescent dye previously applied at earlier stage 51/52 (Figure 2E, right panel).
evidence: Supported by retrograde labeling and immunochemistry data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Early non-ACh appendicular motoneurons constitute at least a sub-population of the cholinergic motoneurons that constitute the future mature appendicular motor innervation after metamorphosis.
source: Thus, these double-labeled MNs that innervated the hindlimb at stage 62 were already present at stage 52, before they expressed the cholinergic molecular phenotype. This finding therefore demonstrated that early non-ACh appendicular MNs constitute at least a sub-population of the cholinergic MNs that constitute the future mature appendicular motor innervation after metamorphosis.
evidence: Inferred from retrograde labeling experiment showing continuity of motoneuron population

claim: ChAT-negative neurons labeled with retrograde dye from the hindlimb bud at larvae younger than stage 55 were strongly Islet1/2-positive.
source: Double immunostaining in larvae younger than stage 55 revealed that the ChAT-negative neurons labeled with retrograde dye applied in the hindlimb bud were also strongly Islet1/2-positive, similar to the mature axial MNs present in the same slices (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunochemistry data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Stage 52 appendicular motoneurons had average resting membrane potential values of −40.2 ± 8.2 mV with low [Cl−] patch solutions.
source: These recorded MNs had average resting membrane potential values of −40.2 ± 8.2 mV (n = 12) and −54.8 ± 2.3 mV (n = 5) with low and high [Cl−] patch solutions, respectively, and were able to produce action potentials either in response to increasing steps of depolarizing current injection (Figure 3C, left), on rebound after release from experimental hyperpolarization (Figure 3C, right) or even spontaneously (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3C-D

claim: Stage 52 appendicular motoneurons were able to produce action potentials in response to increasing steps of depolarizing current injection.
source: These recorded MNs had average resting membrane potential values of −40.2 ± 8.2 mV (n = 12) and −54.8 ± 2.3 mV (n = 5) with low and high [Cl−] patch solutions, respectively, and were able to produce action potentials either in response to increasing steps of depolarizing current injection (Figure 3C, left), on rebound after release from experimental hyperpolarization (Figure 3C, right) or even spontaneously (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3C

claim: During spontaneous episodes of locomotor-like activity, correlated synaptic fluctuations were observed in all identified appendicular motoneurons.
source: Significantly, moreover, during spontaneous episodes of locomotor-like activity monitored from a more caudal spinal ventral root, correlated synaptic fluctuations were observed in all identified appendicular MNs, thereby indicating a functional synaptic coupling with other components of the spinal locomotor network (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Appendicular motoneurons are capable of locomotor-related action potential firing.
source: In addition, the use of an elevated [Cl−] solution in the intracellular electrode (see Materials and methods) revealed a capability for locomotor-related action potential firing in all recorded MNs (Figure 3F), and was consistent with the idea that chloride-mediated signaling was still not fully mature in limb MNs and remained excitatory at early developmental stages (Hanson and Landmesser, 2003; Akerman and Cline, 2006).
evidence: Supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3F and citations

claim: During episodes of spontaneous axial fictive swimming in a stage 53 preparation, locomotor commands monitored from a caudal spinal ventral root elicited rhythmic EMG activity in both the segmental myotomes and limb bud muscles.
source: During episodes of spontaneous axial fictive swimming in a stage 53 preparation (n = 7; Figure 4A, right panel), locomotor commands monitored from a caudal spinal ventral root elicited rhythmic EMG activity in both the segmental myotomes and limb bud muscles.
evidence: Supported by EMG recording data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Under bath application of d-tubocurarine, swimming-related ventral root burst activity persisted, but associated tail myotome EMG activity was completely abolished after 15 min of antagonist perfusion.
source: Under subsequent bath application of d-tubocurarine to block any nicotinic receptors and thereby prevent ACh-dependent synaptic transmission (Sillar and Roberts, 1992; 1993), the expression of swimming-related ventral root burst activity persisted, but associated tail myotome EMG activity was completely abolished after 15 min of antagonist perfusion (Figure 4B,d-tubocurarine).
evidence: Supported by EMG recording data shown in Figure 4B and citations

claim: After >30 min d-tubocurarine perfusion, the hindlimb bud muscles continued to exhibit rhythmic EMG discharges that remained strictly coordinated with the ongoing axial pattern.
source: In contrast, even after >30 min d-tubocurarine perfusion the hindlimb bud muscles continued to exhibit rhythmic EMG discharges that, although reduced in amplitude (see below), remained strictly coordinated with the ongoing axial pattern (Figure 4B,d-tubocurarine; see black arrow in lower middle plot).
evidence: Supported by EMG recording data shown in Figure 4B

claim: In stage 56 preparations, a 15 min bath application of d-tubocurarine completely abolished EMG activity in both the hindlimb bud muscles and tail myotomes.
source: In these cases, however, a 15 min bath application of d-tubocurarine decreased the frequency of the centrally-generated axial swim pattern, and completely abolished, albeit reversibly, associated EMG activity in both the hindlimb bud muscles and tail myotomes (Figure 4C,d-tubocurarine; wash).
evidence: Supported by EMG recording data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Co-localized sites of VAChT and synapsin labeling were found on the somata of identified limb motoneurons.
source: Co-localized sites of VAChT and synapsin labeling were found on the somata of identified limb MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which also expressed calcium fluorescence changes associated with bouts of fictive swimming (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Limb motoneurons expressed calcium fluorescence changes associated with bouts of fictive swimming.
source: Co-localized sites of VAChT and synapsin labeling were found on the somata of identified limb MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which also expressed calcium fluorescence changes associated with bouts of fictive swimming (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: The amplitudes of calcium signals in limb motoneurons were drastically reduced in the presence of d-tubocurarine.
source: Significantly, moreover, the amplitudes of these calcium signals were drastically reduced in the added presence of d-tubocurarine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: At stage 52, there was a total lack of labeling for α-bungarotoxin in hindlimb buds, indicating an absence of muscle ACh receptors at this stage.
source: At stage 52, there was a total lack of labeling for α-bungarotoxin in hindlimb buds (Figure 5A, upper panels), indicating an absence of muscle ACh receptors at this stage.
evidence: Supported by α-bungarotoxin labeling data shown in Figure 5A

claim: At stage 52, diffuse NR2b fluorescence, indicative of glutamate receptor labeling, was observed in the vicinity of motoneuron axons.
source: In contrast, at the same developmental stage, diffuse NR2b fluorescence, indicative of glutamate receptor labeling, was observed in the vicinity of MN axons visualized with neurofilament immuno-detection.
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data

claim: At stage 52, both the axons and cell bodies of limb motoneurons strongly expressed the vesicular glutamate transporter VGluT1.
source: In addition, at stage 52, both the axons (Figure 5C) and cell bodies of limb MNs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) strongly expressed the vesicular glutamate transporter VGluT1, which again predominantly colocalized with synaptophysin and in the vicinity of postsynaptic NR1 labeling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B1).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: The first α-bungarotoxin positive signal was detected at stage 55 with characteristic dispersed dots.
source: The first α-bungarotoxin positive signal was detected at stage 55 with characteristic dispersed dots (data not shown), as previously described (Marsh-Armstrong et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by α-bungarotoxin labeling data and citation

claim: By stage 57, typical clusters of nicotinic receptors were observed close to appendicular nerve terminal branches.
source: By stage 57, typical clusters of nicotinic receptors were observed close to appendicular nerve terminal branches, and in further direct contrast to younger stages, NR2b (Figure 5A, lower panels) and NR1 receptor subunits (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B2) in hindlimb bud muscle as well as VGluT1 in innervating motor axons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B2) were now absent.
evidence: Supported by α-bungarotoxin labeling data shown in Figure 5A

claim: At stage 57, NR2b and NR1 receptor subunits in hindlimb bud muscle as well as VGluT1 in innervating motor axons were absent.
source: By stage 57, typical clusters of nicotinic receptors were observed close to appendicular nerve terminal branches, and in further direct contrast to younger stages, NR2b (Figure 5A, lower panels) and NR1 receptor subunits (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B2) in hindlimb bud muscle as well as VGluT1 in innervating motor axons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B2) were now absent.
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B2

claim: Single pulse electrical stimulation applied to a limb bud motor nerve elicited EMG responses in the hindlimb bud with a mean latency of 7.8 ± 1.9 ms at stages 52-54.
source: Single pulse electrical stimulation applied to a limb bud motor nerve elicited EMG responses in the hindlimb bud with a mean latency of 7.8 ± 1.9 ms at stages 52–54 (n = 6) and 5.1 ± 2.1 ms at stages 55–57 (n = 6), and a mean amplitude of 0.30 ± 0.01 mV at stages 52–54 and 2.50 ± 0.99 mV at stages 55–57 in normal Ringer's saline.
evidence: Supported by EMG recording data from isolated hindlimb preparations

claim: At stages 52-54, the appendicular nerve stimulus-evoked EMG response was increased by 35 ± 6% following d-tubocurarine application.
source: At stages 52–54, the appendicular nerve stimulus-evoked EMG response was not diminished by subsequent d-tubocurarine application, but rather, was increased by 35 ± 6% (Figure 6B, left; Fig; 6C, left black bar, p>0.01, U = 642.0).
evidence: Supported by EMG recording data shown in Figure 6B-C

claim: At stages 52-54, the hindlimb muscle response was decreased by 44 ± 3% following bath-application of CNQX/AP5.
source: Conversely, the hindlimb muscle response was decreased by 44 ± 3% following bath-application of CNQX/AP5 (Figure 6B, left; Figure 6C, left grey bar, p<0.001, U = 39.5).
evidence: Supported by EMG recording data shown in Figure 6B-C

claim: At stages 55-57, the nerve stimulus-evoked EMG response was decreased by 80 ± 2% under d-tubocurarine perfusion.
source: At stages 55–57 on the other hand, the nerve stimulus-evoked EMG response was decreased by 80 ± 2% under d-tubocurarine perfusion (p<0.001, U = 74.0) but was not significantly affected (p=0.5, U = 522.0) in the presence of CNQX/AP5 (Figure 6B, right; Figure 6C, right black and grey bars, respectively).
evidence: Supported by EMG recording data shown in Figure 6B-C

claim: At stages 55-57, the nerve stimulus-evoked EMG response was not significantly affected in the presence of CNQX/AP5.
source: At stages 55–57 on the other hand, the nerve stimulus-evoked EMG response was decreased by 80 ± 2% under d-tubocurarine perfusion (p<0.001, U = 74.0) but was not significantly affected (p=0.5, U = 522.0) in the presence of CNQX/AP5 (Figure 6B, right; Figure 6C, right black and grey bars, respectively).
evidence: Supported by EMG recording data shown in Figure 6B-C

claim: Functional motoneurons are defined as differentiated neurons that are connected to a central premotor network and activate peripheral muscle using acetylcholine.
source: In vertebrates, functional motoneurons are defined as differentiated neurons that are connected to a central premotor network and activate peripheral muscle using acetylcholine.
evidence: Stated as established definition in vertebrates

claim: Motoneurons and muscles generally develop simultaneously during embryogenesis.
source: Generally, motoneurons and muscles develop simultaneously during embryogenesis.
evidence: Stated as general principle

claim: At metamorphosis onset, spinal neurons retrogradely labeled from the emerging hindlimbs initially express neither choline acetyltransferase nor vesicular acetylcholine transporter.
source: Here, we demonstrate that at metamorphosis onset, spinal neurons retrogradely labeled from the emerging hindlimbs initially express neither choline acetyltransferase nor vesicular acetylcholine transporter.
evidence: Stated as main finding in abstract

claim: Early appendicular motoneurons are positive for the motoneuronal transcription factor Islet1/2.
source: Nevertheless, they are positive for the motoneuronal transcription factor Islet1/2 and exhibit intrinsic and axial locomotor-driven electrophysiological activity.
evidence: Stated as main finding in abstract

claim: Early appendicular motoneurons exhibit intrinsic and axial locomotor-driven electrophysiological activity.
source: Nevertheless, they are positive for the motoneuronal transcription factor Islet1/2 and exhibit intrinsic and axial locomotor-driven electrophysiological activity.
evidence: Stated as main finding in abstract

claim: The early appendicular motoneurons activate developing limb muscles via nicotinic antagonist-resistant, glutamate antagonist-sensitive, neuromuscular synapses.
source: Moreover, the early appendicular motoneurons activate developing limb muscles via nicotinic antagonist-resistant, glutamate antagonist-sensitive, neuromuscular synapses.
evidence: Stated as main finding in abstract

claim: The hindlimb muscles transiently express glutamate, but not nicotinic receptors.
source: Coincidently, the hindlimb muscles transiently express glutamate, but not nicotinic receptors.
evidence: Stated as main finding in abstract

claim: Both pre- and postsynaptic neuromuscular partners switch definitively to typical cholinergic transmitter signaling.
source: Subsequently, both pre- and postsynaptic neuromuscular partners switch definitively to typical cholinergic transmitter signaling.
evidence: Stated as main finding in abstract

claim: The results demonstrate a novel context-dependent re-specification of neurotransmitter phenotype during neuromuscular system development.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate a novel context-dependent re-specification of neurotransmitter phenotype during neuromuscular system development.
evidence: Stated as main conclusion in abstract

claim: In mammals, motoneuron specification begins in the ventral neural tube with the induction of progenitors by sonic hedgehog proteins.
source: In mammals, motoneuron (MN) specification begins in the ventral neural tube with the induction of progenitors by sonic hedgehog proteins (Roelink et al., 1995), the graded concentration of which triggers the subsequent expression of specific post-mitotic transcription factors (Goulding, 1998; Jessell, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Roelink et al., 1995; Goulding, 1998; Jessell, 2000

claim: The homeodomain-containing protein Islet1 is the first molecular marker of motoneuron differentiation.
source: The homeodomain-containing protein Islet1 is the first molecular marker of MN differentiation (Ericson et al., 1992) and induces the later expression of homeobox Hb9, which consolidates the motoneuronal phenotype and participates in MN migration and central motor column formation (Arber et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ericson et al., 1992; Arber et al., 1999

claim: Soon after their specification, motoneurons express choline-acetyltransferase (ChAT) and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT).
source: Soon after their specification, MNs express the two typical proteins associated with cholinergic neurotransmission, choline-acetyltransferase (ChAT) and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT), enabling them thereafter to activate their muscle targets (Phelps et al., 1991; Chen and Chiu, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Phelps et al., 1991; Chen and Chiu, 1992

claim: Muscles develop concomitantly with motoneurons and contribute to motoneuron axon path-finding.
source: The muscles, which develop concomitantly and contribute to motoneuron axon path-finding, also play a fundamental role in MN phenotyping and survival (Yin and Oppenheim, 1992; Kablar and Belliveau, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yin and Oppenheim, 1992; Kablar and Belliveau, 2005

claim: Motoneurons are considered to be fully functional once they have become affiliated to a corresponding central motor network and provide impulse-elicited excitation to muscle fibers using acetylcholine as the neurotransmitter.
source: Finally, MNs are considered to be fully functional once they have become affiliated to a corresponding central motor network and provide impulse-elicited excitation to muscle fibers using acetylcholine (ACh) as the neurotransmitter (Davis-Dusenbery et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davis-Dusenbery et al., 2014

claim: In Xenopus laevis, axial motoneurons develop during pre-hatchling embryonic stages and control larval undulatory tail-based swimming.
source: In the amphibian Xenopus laevis, the axial and appendicular MNs controlling tail and limb muscles respectively are generated during two separate developmental periods. The former develop during pre-hatchling embryonic stages and control larval undulatory tail-based swimming by projecting to and exciting axial myotomes via nicotinic ACh receptor activation (van Mier et al., 1985; Sharpe and Goldstone, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Mier et al., 1985; Sharpe and Goldstone, 2000

claim: Motoneurons of the neuromuscular system responsible for limb-based locomotion differentiate and the limb buds start developing during early metamorphosis.
source: In contrast, MNs of the neuromuscular system responsible for later limb-based locomotion differentiate and the limb buds start developing during early metamorphosis (Marsh-Armstrong et al., 2004), when the axial MNs and tail muscles are already entirely developed and operational.
evidence: Supported by citation to Marsh-Armstrong et al., 2004

claim: Glutamate is the predominant excitatory neurotransmitter in the vertebrate CNS.
source: On the other hand, glutamate is the predominant excitatory neurotransmitter in the vertebrate CNS, and supraspinal glutamatergic neurons can re-specify functional glutamatergic NMJs from otherwise purely cholinergic synapses on mammalian skeletal muscles following grafting with transected peripheral motor nerve (Brunelli et al., 2005).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge and supported by citation to Brunelli et al., 2005

claim: Glutamate is a major excitatory neurotransmitter at the NMJ of phylogenetically distant invertebrates.
source: Given such a short-term reorganizing capability and the fact that glutamate is a major excitatory neurotransmitter at the NMJ of phylogenetically distant invertebrates (Gerschenfeld, 1973), it is possible that the transient employment of glutamatergic neuromuscular transmission in pre-metamorphosing Xenopus is representative of a latent ancestral step in the evolutionary transition of intrinsic molecular programming of the NMJ to cholinergic-dependent signaling.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gerschenfeld, 1973

claim: Thyroid hormones control the developmental expression of ChAT.
source: The signal for such neurotransmitter re-specification remains to be determined, but thyroid hormones, which control the developmental expression of ChAT (Patel et al., 1987; Gould and Butcher, 1989) and probably also VAChT since both proteins share the same gene locus (Eiden, 1998), are most likely to be involved.
evidence: Supported by citations to Patel et al., 1987; Gould and Butcher, 1989; Eiden, 1998

claim: ChAT and VAChT share the same gene locus.
source: The signal for such neurotransmitter re-specification remains to be determined, but thyroid hormones, which control the developmental expression of ChAT (Patel et al., 1987; Gould and Butcher, 1989) and probably also VAChT since both proteins share the same gene locus (Eiden, 1998), are most likely to be involved.
evidence: Supported by citation to Eiden, 1998

claim: The increase in thyroid hormone levels at metamorphosis onset starts at stage 54-55 in Xenopus.
source: Consistent with this possibility is that the increase in thyroid hormone levels at metamorphosis onset, which starts at stage 54–55 in Xenopus (Shi, 2000), triggers a variety of gene-switching molecular programs required for the development of limb muscles and associated motor circuitry through the regulation of spinal cord neurogenesis and functions (Das et al., 2002; Marsh-Armstrong et al., 2004; Brown et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shi, 2000; Das et al., 2002; Marsh-Armstrong et al., 2004; Brown et al., 2005

claim: A developmental shift in the mechanism by which the appendicular motoneurons activate their target muscles during fictive locomotion occurs around stages 54-55.
source: The differential effects of d-tubocurarine at early and later larval stages also suggested that a developmental shift in the mechanism by which the appendicular MNs activate their target muscles during fictive locomotion occurs around intervening stages 54–55.
evidence: Inferred from differential pharmacological effects at different developmental stages

claim: Neurotransmitter phenotype switching can maintain or invert synaptic sign and is generally associated with observable behavioral changes.
source: This loss/gain in pre-synaptic neurotransmitter/post-synaptic receptor phenotype has been reported to occur in developmental, post-lesional or activity-dependent contexts and is considered to be a major underlying feature of neuronal plasticity (Spitzer, 2017). It can either maintain or invert synaptic sign (Borodinsky et al., 2004; Borodinsky and Spitzer, 2007) and is generally associated with observable behavioral changes (Sillar et al., 1998; Demarque and Spitzer, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Spitzer, 2017; Borodinsky et al., 2004; Borodinsky and Spitzer, 2007; Sillar et al., 1998; Demarque and Spitzer, 2010

claim: The transient employment of glutamatergic neuromuscular transmission in pre-metamorphosing Xenopus may be representative of a latent ancestral step in the evolutionary transition of intrinsic molecular programming of the NMJ to cholinergic-dependent signaling.
source: Given such a short-term reorganizing capability and the fact that glutamate is a major excitatory neurotransmitter at the NMJ of phylogenetically distant invertebrates (Gerschenfeld, 1973), it is possible that the transient employment of glutamatergic neuromuscular transmission in pre-metamorphosing Xenopus is representative of a latent ancestral step in the evolutionary transition of intrinsic molecular programming of the NMJ to cholinergic-dependent signaling.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on evolutionary considerations

claim: A matched expression of glutamatergic neurotransmitter and receptors in appendicular motoneurons and limb muscles during pre-metamorphosis could ensure the correct orientation of the developing axon growth cones towards the limb buds.
source: On the contrary, a matched expression of glutamatergic neurotransmitter and receptors in appendicular MNs and limb muscles during pre-metamorphosis could ensure the correct orientation of the developing axon growth cones towards the limb buds and the establishment of synaptic contacts appropriate for the control of limb movements (Figure 7A).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the functional significance of glutamatergic signaling

claim: Xenopus laevis possesses two genes for ChAT that exhibit about 87% nucleotide identity.
source: Because of its tetraploid status, X. laevis possesses two genes for ChAT (Genbank accession numbers: XM_018225547 and XM_018239425 for ChAT1 and ChAT2, respectively) that exhibit about 87% nucleotide identity.
evidence: Stated as fact about Xenopus laevis genome
